implementation_notes: On a broker the property section is a first-class user-property bag: Azure Service Bus exposes application-defined key-value pairs (mapped to AMQP application-properties and to HTTP headers) that subscription rules can filter on, and NServiceBus stamps the message type into the NServiceBus.EnclosedMessageTypes header so the endpoint selects its deserialiser before the body. System.Text.Json itself provides no such channel - its polymorphism support writes a $type discriminator into the document, which is the content-based sibling - so the property channel always comes from the transport or the messaging framework. Prefer the framework header when the endpoint already uses NServiceBus; otherwise set a user property explicitly.
pitfalls: Dynamic type loading and content-based type inference (Json.NET TypeNameHandling) let the incoming message choose its own type; both can be disabled, and NServiceBus documents the switches - do so and require the header.
User properties are typed through the AMQP mapping and only a subset can be used in broker rules, so a token the rule engine cannot compare silently never matches.
Forwarding or re-sending drops application properties when the code builds a new message instead of copying them.
